title: The flying Sikh
hook: Milkha Singh, a Partition orphan, became a famous sprinter

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Sikh prime minister, and your line was quiet service. Whose quiet work in public life did you notice? Today, a man who was anything but quiet on a running track. Day one thousand nineteen.

Running came into Milkha Singh's life long before any race. In the violence of Partition, by his own telling, a boy ran for his life while his village was attacked behind him. He lost his parents and others of his family, and he arrived in Delhi a refugee with nothing. Years later the same boy would be running again, on cinder tracks, in front of crowds, with a nickname that followed him for the rest of his life. Today: the flying Sikh.
screen: `A BOY RUNNING FOR HIS LIFE.` → `A REFUGEE WITH NOTHING.` → `THE FLYING SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the loss. In his autobiography, Milkha Singh describes Partition taking his parents and others he loved, and the hunger and drifting that came after, in camps and on city streets. He doesn't make it pretty. Second, the army. He joined the Indian Army, and it was there, he says, that he found out he could run. A race for soldiers, a reward of extra milk, then more races, then training that he describes as brutal and lonely. A body that had run for its life learned to run for something else. Third, the race in Pakistan. He tells how he was invited to race in Lahore, across the new border, in the land where his family had been killed. At first he refused. He was persuaded to go. He ran, and won, and in his telling it was there that he was called the flying Sikh. The name came from the other side of the line. Fourth, the root. In Gujri ki Var, at Ang 522 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says: keep making the effort, and you will live; keep working, and you will taste peace; keep remembering the Lord, and worry falls away. Effort, work and remembrance, side by side. It doesn't say loss is good, or that Partition was a gift. It says the next step is still yours to take. Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits that keep climbing even after loss. Milkha Singh's story doesn't erase what he lost. It shows what he ran toward anyway. That's today's line: from orphan to athlete.
screen: `A FAMILY LOST AT PARTITION.` · `THE ARMY, AND A RACE FOR MILK.` · `A RACE ACROSS THE NEW BORDER.` · `KEEP MAKING THE EFFORT.` · then, large: `FROM ORPHAN TO ATHLETE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in your legs. Sit with both feet flat on the floor. Press them down gently, and feel the muscles in your calves and thighs wake up. Breathe in, and remember a time you ran or walked fast just for the joy of it, as a child or last week. Breathe out, and bring to mind one hard thing in your past that you carried forward instead of leaving behind. Let the two sit side by side: the hard thing and the moving legs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each step you imagine. The bell holds the time.
The flying Sikh. Milkha Singh, who lost his parents at Partition, found his speed in the army, and was given the name after a race in Lahore. Today's word.
Your line: from orphan to athlete. Today, run or walk briskly for a few minutes, wherever you are, and let your body remember it can move forward. Day one thousand nineteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of chardi kala, rising spirits even after loss, and stories like Milkha Singh's are told in families and gurdwaras as examples of carrying on after Partition.
